items.title: Neutral Reading
items.question: What is the pH of pure water at room temperature?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 7. Pure water sits at the midpoint of the scale, neither acidic nor basic.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 7. The midpoint marks neutrality because hydrogen and hydroxide ions are balanced.
items.lessonContent:
Scales have meaningful midpoints.
Balance of ions defines neutrality.
Know the reference value.
Compare other readings against it.
Share this: find the neutral point on one scale you use.

items.title: Sour Fruit
items.question: Approximately what pH does lemon juice have?
items.correctExplanation: About 2. Its sharp sourness comes from a strongly acidic solution.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Taste and pH usually agree, which is why sour foods read low on the scale.
items.lessonContent:
Sensory cues can hint at chemistry.
Sourness often signals acidity.
Estimate before measuring.
Confirm with an indicator.
Share this: guess the acidity of one sour food you eat.

items.title: Baking Soda
items.question: Approximately what pH does a baking soda solution have?
items.correctExplanation: About 9. It sits mildly on the basic side of the scale.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 9. Baking soda neutralises acids, which is a sign it is basic rather than acidic.
items.lessonContent:
Function reveals chemical character.
Neutralisers are usually basic.
Estimate from behaviour.
Test with an indicator to confirm.
Share this: name one kitchen ingredient used to neutralise acid.

items.title: Sour Liquid
items.question: Approximately what pH does household vinegar have?
items.correctExplanation: About 3. Vinegar is acidic, though less so than lemon juice.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. The single unit above lemon juice means it is about ten times less acidic.
items.lessonContent:
Small scale differences matter.
Compare similar substances by units.
Estimate before checking.
Use relative acidity in reasoning.
Share this: rank two sour liquids by guessed acidity.

items.title: Slippery Bar
items.question: A bar of soap leaves a slippery feel on the skin. Roughly where does its solution sit on the scale?
items.correctExplanation: About 10. Soap is basic, which is why it feels slippery on the skin.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. The slippery feel is a sensory clue to a solution on the basic side.
items.lessonContent:
Touch can hint at chemistry.
Slippery substances tend to be basic.
Pair sensation with measurement.
Notice consistent everyday clues.
Share this: compare how soap and lemon feel on your hands.

items.title: Stomach Fluid
items.question: Approximately what pH does human stomach acid have?
items.correctExplanation: About 1. It is among the most acidic fluids in the body, strong enough to break down food.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. The extreme acidity is why the stomach lining must constantly renew itself.
items.lessonContent:
Extreme conditions serve functions.
Protective linings guard against chemistry.
High acidity aids digestion.
Connect environment to purpose.
Share this: note one body environment built for a harsh condition.

items.title: Mild Drink
items.question: Approximately what pH does fresh milk have?
items.correctExplanation: About 6. Milk is very slightly acidic, close to neutral.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Sitting just below the midpoint, it is only faintly acidic.
items.lessonContent:
Values near the middle are easily misjudged.
Small shifts still count.
Estimate before measuring.
Compare against neutrality.
Share this: guess whether milk is acidic or basic, then check.

items.title: Household Bleach
items.question: Bleach is strongly caustic and must be used with ventilation. About what reading does a household bleach solution give?
items.correctExplanation: About 13. It is strongly basic and should be handled with care.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 13. The high reading explains why it is caustic and why ventilation matters.
items.lessonContent:
Extremes carry safety concerns.
High values signal corrosiveness.
Handle strong substances carefully.
Read labels for warnings.
Share this: check the warning on one strong household cleaner.

items.title: Morning Drink
items.question: Approximately what pH does black coffee have?
items.correctExplanation: About 5. Coffee is mildly acidic, which some sensitive stomachs notice.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Its acidity is far milder than vinegar but still below neutral.
items.lessonContent:
Common drinks vary in acidity.
Mild values still affect sensitive people.
Estimate before measuring.
Relate chemistry to comfort.
Share this: rank your favourite drinks by guessed acidity.

items.title: Red Fruit
items.question: Tomato juice resists spoilage thanks to its own chemistry. Approximately what value does it read?
items.correctExplanation: About 4. Tomato juice is acidic enough to be used in preserving.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. The acidity helps resist spoilage, which is why it appears in canning recipes.
items.lessonContent:
Acidity affects preservation.
Chemistry has practical kitchen uses.
Estimate before checking.
Connect a property to its purpose.
Share this: name one food preserved by its own acidity.

items.title: One Step
items.question: By what factor does acidity change when the pH drops by one unit?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 10. The scale is logarithmic, so one unit represents a tenfold change.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. Reading the scale as linear seriously underestimates the differences between values.
items.lessonContent:
Some scales are logarithmic.
A single unit can mean a large change.
Do not read such scales linearly.
Respect hidden multipliers.
Share this: find one everyday scale that is not linear.

items.title: Two Steps
items.question: If one unit means a tenfold change, what does a two-unit drop represent?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 100. Each unit multiplies by ten, so two units multiply by ten twice.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 100. Two units are not twice the change but a hundredfold one.
items.lessonContent:
Logarithmic scales compound.
Each step multiplies the last.
Use powers for repeated multipliers.
Avoid linear intuition here.
Share this: compute the change across two steps of a tenfold scale.

items.title: Below Seven
items.question: What term describes any solution with a pH below seven?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Values below the midpoint mean an excess of hydrogen ions.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is acidic. The lower the number, the stronger the acidity.
items.lessonContent:
A threshold divides a scale.
Direction from the midpoint matters.
Use consistent terminology.
Classify before comparing.
Share this: classify three liquids as above or below neutral.

items.title: Above Seven
items.question: What label applies to a solution whose value is greater than the neutral midpoint?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Values above the midpoint mean an excess of hydroxide ions.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is basic. The higher the number, the stronger the basicity.
items.lessonContent:
The upper half has its own name.
Direction from neutral defines it.
Keep terms precise.
Classify by position.
Share this: identify one basic liquid in your kitchen.

items.title: Exactly Seven
items.question: What word describes a solution sitting exactly at the neutral midpoint?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. At the midpoint the two opposing ions balance exactly.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is neutral. It is neither acidic nor basic, which is why it serves as the reference point.
items.lessonContent:
Balance defines a midpoint.
Reference points anchor a scale.
Neither extreme describes the middle.
Use the centre for comparison.
Share this: find one quantity that represents a natural balance point.

items.title: Paper Colour
items.question: What colour does blue litmus paper turn in an acidic solution?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Blue litmus turning red is the classic indicator test for acidity.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is red. The colour change shows that the solution carries an excess of hydrogen ions.
items.lessonContent:
Indicators make invisible chemistry visible.
A colour change signals a shift.
Learn the standard tests.
Choose a test that gives a clear result.
Share this: use a natural indicator like red cabbage to test a liquid.

items.title: Other Colour
items.question: What colour does red litmus paper turn in a basic solution?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Red litmus turning blue is the standard indicator test for a base.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is blue. The two litmus colours map cleanly onto the two halves of the scale.
items.lessonContent:
Tests come in complementary pairs.
One change can confirm the opposite condition.
Learn both directions.
Use simple tools well.
Share this: predict the litmus change before testing a liquid.

items.title: Neutralising Pair
items.question: What two products form when an acid reacts with a base?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The opposing ions combine, leaving a dissolved salt in water.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is salt and water. The reaction cancels both characters rather than strengthening either.
items.lessonContent:
Opposites can cancel.
Reactions yield new substances.
Predict products from reactants.
Balance matters in combining reagents.
Share this: name one everyday neutralisation you have seen.

items.title: Acid on Metal
items.question: What gas is usually released when an acid reacts with a reactive metal?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Bubbles of this light gas appear, which can be collected and tested.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is hydrogen. The escaping gas is why metals fizz when acid is poured over them.
items.lessonContent:
Reactions release identifiable products.
Bubbles are a sign of gas production.
Predict products from known patterns.
Observe evidence of reactions.
Share this: recall one reaction that produces visible bubbles.

items.title: Acid on Carbonate
items.question: What gas fizzes off when an acid reacts with a carbonate?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. This gas turns limewater cloudy, a classic test for it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is carbon dioxide gas. The same gas appears in baking, where acid meets carbonate to raise dough.
items.lessonContent:
Reactions can be identified by their gases.
Tests confirm which gas is present.
Recognise patterns across contexts.
Connect evidence to conclusion.
Share this: notice the fizz in one baking or cleaning reaction.

items.title: Stronger of Two
items.question: Which is more acidic, a solution of pH two or one of pH five?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The lower number means a thousandfold greater acidity because the scale is logarithmic.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is pH 2. The larger-looking number is actually the weaker acid, since lower values mean stronger acidity.
items.lessonContent:
Lower values can mean more, not less.
Read the direction of a scale carefully.
Logarithmic gaps are large.
Compare after understanding the scale.
Share this: check the direction of one scale before comparing two readings.

items.title: Acid Particle
items.question: Which ion is responsible for acidic behaviour in solution?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. More of these positively charged particles make a solution more acidic.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is hydrogen ions. Acidity is defined by their concentration relative to the opposing ions.
items.lessonContent:
Behaviour traces to particles.
Ions drive acid and base character.
Name the microscopic cause.
Connect concentration to observation.
Share this: link one visible property to an invisible cause.

items.title: Base Particle
items.question: Which negatively charged particle gives a solution its basic character?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. More of these negatively charged particles make a solution more basic.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is hydroxide ions. They balance against hydrogen ions, and the winner sets the character.
items.lessonContent:
Two ions define a tug of war.
The majority sets the character.
Think in terms of balance.
Name both sides of a contrast.
Share this: compare the two ions behind one familiar scale.

items.title: Resisting Change
items.question: What is a solution called that resists changes in pH when acid or base is added?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. A buffer absorbs added acid or base to hold the pH fairly steady.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a buffer. Living systems depend on this stabilising action to keep conditions safe.
items.lessonContent:
Stability can be engineered.
Some systems resist disruption.
Balance mechanisms protect conditions.
Look for what maintains a range.
Share this: find one system that keeps a value steady against disturbance.

items.title: Usual Bounds
items.question: What range of values does the standard pH scale usually span?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The familiar scale runs from strongly acidic at the bottom to strongly basic at the top.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 0 to 14. Extremely concentrated solutions can fall outside it, so the range is a convenience.
items.lessonContent:
Conventional ranges are useful, not absolute.
Know the usual bounds.
Recognise when a scale is exceeded.
Do not treat convention as a law.
